column1: # Final acceptance manifest for the Scripture chronology corpus.
# The complete review surface for a GENUINELY COLD acceptance review:
# a new agent or session that performed none of the population, the
# first audit, the post-audit correction, the targeted re-review, or
# the repair that closed its 23 failures. Every row is reviewed.
# Derived from two production diffs -- 2330d63a5..214797e78 and
# 214797e78..eb38161ba -- by loading each revision's corpus through its
# OWN scripts/_chronology.py and diffing the loaded OBJECTS, so a
# reformat cannot hide a change and a loader that has since tightened
# cannot refuse to read the older side. Deduplicated on
# case_type + ':' + claim_or_scope_id. Nothing is sampled and nothing
# which fails on any changed case this file omits, any row no diff
# supports, and any prior review id no row cites.

column11: Gigot, "Daniel", CE vol. 4 (1908), the biographical section: "carried captive to Babylon by Nabuchodonosor in the fourth year of the reign of Joakim (605 B.C.)" and "Daniel continued to prosper through the rest of the reign of Darius, and in that of his successor, Cyrus the Persian"

column11: Eusebius, Church History II.10.9, the death of Agrippa

column11: Howlett, "Biblical Chronology", CE vol. 3 (1908), section "The apostles": "Perhaps we may say 62, for he was sent to Rome by Festus, shortly after his arrival in Judea . But this was not long before the death of Pallas in A.D. 62"; and the section head, Blass on ten years
column13: The substantive fix carried the article's hedge onto the begin endpoint, which is right; the edit also left a second identical sources: key inside the same claim mapping. PyYAML keeps the last silently, so validate passed over a file that is not valid YAML 1.2 - a corpus that reads healthy while being machine-invalid is the exact shape this apparatus exists to catch, and a round-tripping loader would reject the file outright.
column14: python3 tools/tpt scripture-chronology validate must now refuse a repeated key by file, line and name (see guidance 16), so re-run it and then prove the gate bites by adding a duplicate key to a scratch copy of events.yaml and loading that copy. Then python3 .scratch/cold-audit/src.py artifact.catholic-encyclopedia.volume-3.new-york-1908.newadvent-03731a-f5f96f04 -g 'Perhaps we may say' and check the basis reproduces the sentence including the source's own space before the full stop after 'Judea'.

column11: Josue 11:18 ("Josue made war a long time against these kings"), 11:23 and 4:19 in the tracked Douay
column13: The claim had put an unquantified length ("a long time") inside a relative offset payload, so a length was standing where a distance from an anchor belongs; the statement and label now state sequence only. Section 10.0 makes that distinction structural because one value meaning both is a date that resolves successfully and wrongly.

Then read Jos 11:18, 11:23 and 4:19 with python3 -c "import json;print(json.load(open('src/sources/bibles/douay-rheims/chapters/Jos/11.json'))['verses']['18'])" and check the corpus says only what the verses say about order.

column11: Howlett, "Biblical Chronology": "But the traditional date is 975"; and the Petavius table reproduced in Sloet's "Chronology of the Kings"
column13: The preferred claim's note used to justify its preference by contrast with 'the competing figures' - the two Howlett figures now withdrawn - so it had to be rewritten or it would have been describing claims that no longer exist. What the note now rests the preference on is that the article itself calls 975 the traditional date and that Petavius independently sets Roboam there. If that is not what the sources say, the profile's first answer for the division of the kingdom is preferred on a reason nobody can check.

Then python3 .scratch/cold-audit/src.py artifact.catholic-encyclopedia.volume-3.new-york-1908.newadvent-03731a-f5f96f04 -g 'traditional date' and check the article's own words, and confirm the Petavius figure in Sloet's article independently.

column10: artifact.catholic-encyclopedia.volume-3.new-york-1908.newadvent-03731a-f5f96f04; Sloet, "Chronology of the Kings", Catholic Encyclopedia vol. 8
column11: Sloet's table, drawn up "in conjunction with the data of profane history", B.C. 933-2; and the Petavius table setting Roboam at B.C. 975
column13: This is an index-shift row: with the 936 and 937 withdrawn, Sloet's B.C. 933-2 moved from index 4 to index 2 and the object diff reports date, label, sources, basis, note, precision and endpoints as changed. Nothing about the claim moved. A reviewer who reads the change list literally will look for a re-dating that did not happen, and one who does not check will not notice that Sloet's table is now the only competing figure the event holds - and that it is drawn up on profane history, which is the same objection the withdrawn figures fell to.

Then rule on the escalation the repair lane left open: Sloet's table says of itself that it is drawn up in conjunction with the data of profane history, and the lane withdrew Howlett's figures for less.

column11: Howlett, "Biblical Chronology", "Building of the Temple to its destruction": "We have fixed roughly the date of the revolt of the Ten Tribes for the year 936 B.C. But the traditional date is 975"
column13: Howlett's 936 is withdrawn. The same sentence that gives it names 975 as the traditional date, and the corpus keeps the 975 and displays it first - so this row is where the profile boundary is at its sharpest: one sentence, two figures, one admitted and one not, on the article's own distinction between its reckoning and the tradition.
column14: python3 tools/tpt scripture-chronology query 3Kings.12.19 --json: no 936 and no 937, the preferred claim must be the 975 the article itself calls traditional. Then python3 .scratch/cold-audit/src.py artifact.catholic-encyclopedia.volume-3.new-york-1908.newadvent-03731a-f5f96f04 -g 'traditional date is 975' and read the derivation that reaches 936 from the about 969; check the subject note records both withdrawn figures.

column11: Howlett, "Biblical Chronology": "We conclude then that the Temple was built about 969. The secession of the Ten Tribes took place about 937."
column13: The 'about 937' is withdrawn with the 936 it contradicts by one year. Both descend from the about 969; keeping either would have rebuilt the defect the ruling condemns. If the two are genuinely independent of the Assyrian reckoning, two sourced figures have been deleted.
column14: python3 tools/tpt scripture-chronology query 3Kings.12.19 --json and confirm neither 936 nor 937 survives. column13: The relative statement and the label had spliced Ezech 1:1 to 1:2 with no mark, so a consumer read as one continuous quotation a string the text does not print continuously. An unmarked elision inside quotation marks is a misquotation whatever the substance, and this one is on the anchor for the whole Ezechiel dating chain.

Then python3 tools/tpt scripture-chronology query Ezech.1.1 --json and confirm the anchor is israel.exile.second-captivity and that the label reads as a quotation and not as a paraphrase.

column11: Ezechiel 24:15-18 in the tracked Douay; Schets, "Ezekiel", CE vol. 5 (1909), the paragraph grouping the two words of chapter 24
column13: The claim is withdrawn and the event stands claimless. Its relative anchor was israel.exile.ezechiel.ministry, which is the event's own parent - a container returned by Date.anchor as though the episode were counted from the span's start, which guidance 10.0's 'Containment is not offset' exists to prevent. An earlier ledger withdrew the finding on the ground that an event must carry a non-empty dates list; the loader does not impose that, and saul-accession had already been standing claimless in the same file. Nothing false was ever displayed, so what is at stake is whether the corpus encodes what its sources actually say.
column14: python3 tools/tpt scripture-chronology query Ezech.24.18 --json: the locus must still answer dated from the inherited Ezech-scoped claims, the narrated-event binding over Ezech 24:18-20 must survive, and no assertion may carry an anchor. Then read the event note and check the verbatim Ezech 24:16-18 text against python3 -c "import json;d=json.load(open('src/sources/bibles/douay-rheims/chapters/Ezech/24.json'));print(d['verses']['16'],d['verses']['17'],d['verses']['18'])". Confirm the general rule was NOT adopted: five other claims legitimately anchor on their own parent and each states a real position against it, so check those five still load and still say something about their anchor.

column11: Haydock note at Ps 70:1, artifact PDF page 776 (printed p. 740): the clause 'the second, under Jechonias, 3405'
column13: The A.M. 3405 figure was preferred and is now alternate, because Scripture's own statement at 4 Kings 24:12 was never authored and a rank-6-via-rank-3 reported figure was standing in the profile's first slot. Section 4.2 says a higher rank never yields to a lower one; if the demotion is wrong the corpus has buried its best-sourced claim, and if the demotion is right but incomplete the profile still answers from Ussher through Haydock.
column14: python3 tools/tpt scripture-chronology query 4Kings.24.12 --json: exactly one claim may be preferred, and it must be the Scripture claim. Then read page 776 of the Haydock facsimile and check the basis quotes the whole printed sentence rather than a slice of it, which is what findings LEAD-002 and E2-007 were about.

It is a relative date anchored on israel.exile.nabuchodonosor-accession; if the anchor is not where Scripture puts the eighth year, the corpus has replaced a sourced figure with a wrong one and called it Scripture's own.
